title: Four cubits (Berakhot 8a)
hookLine: since the Temple fell, God has only the four cubits of halakha in the world
tomorrow: a sword at your neck. is it too late to ask?

cards: A new apartment, half the size of the old house. Boxes on every surface, and one question nobody can answer yet: where does everything go? A grandfather sits on a sealed box and says it's fine.
Berakhot asks a bigger version of it. The Temple, God's house, is gone. Where does God live now?

teach.b: The answer, given in Ulla's name, is startlingly small: since the day the Temple was destroyed, the Holy One has nothing in the world but the four cubits of halakha.
A cubit is an old measure, about the length of a forearm, and some readers picture four of them as the space around one person. Halakha is the Jewish way of living, the law walked out day by day.
So the house of God shrinks, and lands in a space the size of a person doing the right thing. That changed how one sage lived. Abaye says: at first I used to study at home and pray in the synagogue.
Once I heard this, I prayed only where I studied. The place where the learning happens became the holy place.

teach.h: GOD'S PLACE: FOUR CUBITS OF HALAKHA.
teach.b: Here's one to tell a friend tonight: in the Talmud, after the Temple fell, God's whole place in the world became four cubits.
That sounds like loss, and it is; the page doesn't pretend otherwise.
Four cubits fit in a dorm room, a kitchen corner, a chair by a hospital bed. Wherever someone sits down to learn and live it, there's room. A Temple-sized absence, and a person-sized answer.

how: Many Jews keep a set place for prayer, a makom kavua, a custom discussed on these same pages of Berakhot, and some keep a small corner at home for study and prayer.

the size of the altar that once stood in the Temple

games.q: your cousin is starting college in a shared dorm room and worries there's no space to practice anything. what does Berakhot 8a offer?
o: four cubits is enough: one small spot where you learn and live it.
wait until she finds a synagogue; a dorm can't be a holy place.
skip it for now; holiness needs its own room in a proper house.
games.why: since the Temple fell, the Talmud says, God's place is four cubits of halakha. a dorm corner is the right size.

practice: Choose one small spot within reach: a corner of a desk, a shelf, a windowsill. Clear it if you can, and set one thing there that stands for what matters to you, a book, a candle, a photo.
Sit facing it for the rest of the sit, and let that small space be enough.

wordCard.voice: Four cubits. After the Temple fell, the Talmud says, God's place in the world became the four cubits of halakha.

orig.note: Hebrew: four cubits; with halakha, God's place in the world after the Temple fell.

carryVoice: One to keep: four cubits, a person-sized room for something holy. That's Berakhot, day nine.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 8a (Rabbi Chiya bar Ami in Ulla's name: since the Temple was destroyed, God has only the four cubits of halakha; Abaye prays where he studies)
